purpose: Map the first aftermath of dying: the body leaving, paperwork, funeral/disposition language, altered household, social speech, grief triggers, children, and the first-year calendar.
principles: Afterward records are witnessed moments, not grief advice.
Administrative burden is part of the phenomenology, not an appendix.
Funeral and disposition language must be jurisdiction-, culture-, and authority-bound.
Grief language must not become a stage model, performance demand, or lay diagnosis.
Objects, children, hidden relationships, and family conflict are identifiability-sensitive by default.

clusters.name: First hours: calls, body, papers, and release
clusters.danger: turning the first hours into a universal checklist or body-handling guide

clusters.name: Administrative aftershock: systems that still address the dead as living
clusters.danger: legal/financial advice and exclusion of chosen kin or unofficial caregivers

clusters.name: Funeral, money, disposition, and public ritual language
clusters.danger: consumer advice, ritual flattening, upsell blindness, and cause-of-death identifiability

clusters.name: Objects, house, body absence, and material grief
clusters.danger: sentimentalizing or exposing identifying object details

clusters.name: Grief grammar: phrases, waves, anticipation, diagnoses, and calendar returns
clusters.danger: pathologizing grief or making a new stage model

clusters.name: Children and young people in the first aftermath
clusters.danger: publishing children's words or forcing adult grief performance

coverage_note: Rev0008 adds 22 quarantined records. It does not yet admit private testimony, public child records, suicide aftermath details, violent/sudden death scenes, custody death, unclaimed bodies, or restricted cultural material.
